piezas.titulo: Which Local LMs are Best For Which Tasks
piezas.resumenOriginal: A local language model is one whose actual weights, the enormous file of learned numbers that constitutes the trained model, you download and run entirely on your own hardware.

destilado.texto: ¿Puede un modelo de lenguaje local superar a los servicios en la nube? Un estudio de KDnuggets muestra que los modelos de lenguaje locales destacan en tareas que requieren privacidad y baja latencia. Por eso, elegir la arquitectura adecuada depende del tipo de tarea que se quiera ejecutar.

piezas.titulo: Neurodiversity Firesides
piezas.resumenOriginal: Neurodiversity Firesides Cwalker Mon, 08/30/2021 - 21:08 Neurodevelopmental therapies are shifting away from a deficit lens to person-centered and respectful practices. It has been exciting to see this referenced in AOTA special issues, trauma informed practice, interpersonal neurobiology and the work of autistic educators and self-advocates. As we celebrate diversity and different ways of being, we truly embrace the concept of "different not less" and principles of actualization that are central to the provision of health care. How do we hold on to these key principles and move away from archaic and outmoded treatment models? How do we resist socialization into the pathology model and challenge our own ableism and biases? Join Virginia Spielmann for these informal and interactive discussions every quarter. Each session is oriented around a theme that informs the clinician's ability to engage in authentic neurodiversity affirming practice and challenge systemic ableism and norm-driven treatment models. Cost: $10 (includes both live-streamed and recorded versions) Presenter: Virginia Spielmann, PhD, OTR/L Executive Director (she/her) Virginia is a well-travelled speaker, coach and educator on topics including sensory integration, DIR/Floortime, child development and infant mental health. She has conducted trainings in Kenya, Australia, the Philippines, Vietnam, Hong Kong, and the USA and leads workshops at international conferences. Virginia is a founder and former Clinical Director of SPOT (Speech, Physical, and Occupational Therapy) Interdisciplinary Children's Therapy Center in Hong Kong, where she led a large and widely respected inter-disciplinary team. Virginia obtained her BSc in Occupational Therapy in Oxford England (2002) and her Masters in Occupational Therapy from Mount Mary University, Milwaukee (2018). She is a DIR/Floortime Training Leader and Expert and clinical consultant for the Interdisciplinary Council for Development and Learning (ICDL). Her extensive pediatric experience includes children on the autism spectrum, as well as those with Sensory Processing Disorder, infant mental health issues, children from adopted families and those who have experienced developmental trauma. Virginia has considerable post-graduate training, she is certified on the SIPT and is currently completing her Ph.D. in Infant and Early Childhood Development with an emphasis on mental health, with Fielding Graduate University, in Santa Barbara. piezas.titulo: A brief neuromotor-therapy-augmented pathway for pediatric functional movement disorders: a sequential historical cohort study
piezas.resumenOriginal: BackgroundPediatric functional movement disorders (FMD) often improve, but access to specialized motor rehabilitation is heterogeneous. We compared two sequential, non-overlapping care periods within one clinical unit: usual care (UC) and a neuromotor-therapy-augmented pathway (NMT-A), which added brief hospital-based neuromotor therapy before community referral.MethodsThis retrospective, non-randomized historical cohort included 17 UC patients (June 2021–January 2023) and 29 NMT-A patients (February 2023–June 2025). The primary outcome was continuous S-FMDRS at 6 months; S-FMDRS-defined motor symptom-free status (score = 0) was secondary. Both were reassessed at 12 months, together with community-treatment engagement.ResultsAt 6 months, the adjusted NMT-A-minus-UC S-FMDRS difference was −1.66 points (95% CI, −4.04 to 0.72). Motor symptom-free status occurred in 55.2% versus 5.9% (risk difference, 49.3 percentage points; 95% CI, 21.8 to 66.4), and in 86.2% versus 52.9% at 12 months (risk difference, 33.3 percentage points; 95% CI, 6.5 to 56.8). The pathway-by-time interaction was not significant. Sustained community physical and/or occupational therapy was documented in 75.0% versus 17.6% (RR, 4.25; 95% CI, 1.74–12.46).ConclusionThe NMT-A pathway-period was associated with more frequent motor symptom-free status and greater continuity of community motor rehabilitation, although the adjusted mean S-FMDRS difference was not statistically significant. Because pathway and calendar period were inseparable, these findings should be interpreted as associations with the overall later care pathway rather than as an isolated effect of NMT.

destilado.texto: No es solo diagnóstico: también es cómo se brinda rehabilitación. piezas.titulo: Cortical responses to lipread and text-based audiovisual stimuli in adults with and without dyslexia
piezas.resumenOriginal: Phonetic recalibration enables listeners to adjust their perception of ambiguous speech sounds based on visual contextual information. In line with a specific difficulty in forming letter-speech sound associations, adults with dyslexia have been found to show no text-based, but intact lipread-based, recalibration. The underlying neural mechanisms remain unclear however. This fMRI study examined cortical responses during text-based and lipread-based phonetic recalibration in 34 adults (18 with dyslexia, 16 typical readers). Participants were exposed to ambiguous speech sounds /a?a/ paired with disambiguating visual information (“aba”/“ada” text or lipread videos), followed by auditory-only categorization trials. Contrary to previous findings, both groups showed robust text-based and lipread-based behavioral recalibration effects, with no significant group differences between typical and dyslexic readers. Neuroimaging data did yield group differences in the underlying cortical activation. Most notably, dyslexic readers demonstrated increased bilateral fusiform activation compared to typical readers during exposure to lipread videos and ambiguous speech sounds, with left fusiform activation specifically correlating with increased phonological processing difficulties. Additionally, typical readers exhibited higher right frontal activation during text-based audiovisual stimuli. These findings suggest that while adults with dyslexia did not differ significantly from typical readers in behavioral recalibration effects, they employed different neural processing strategies. Unexpectedly, this was particularly the case for lipread audiovisual stimuli. The relatively increased fusiform and superior temporal activation to lipread audiovisual stimuli in dyslexic readers possibly relates to subtle difficulties in phonological processing of ambiguous speech signals.

destilado.texto: No es solo una cuestión de percepción: los adultos con dislexia mostraron recalibración fonética tanto con texto como con labios, sin diferencias conductuales respecto a lectores típicos. piezas.titulo: Brain representations of visual short-term memories during healthy human aging: occipital decline and frontoparietal compensation

Decoding was strongest in visual cortex, but also significant in frontoparietal regions, with different profiles. Visual representations weakened with memory load and age, and statistically mediated age-related performance decline, especially during recall. This coupling, however, weakened with age: some older adults retained stronger visual representations than performance implied, suggesting impaired access to a partially preserved memory trace. Frontoparietal representations, instead, were largely insensitive to load and strengthened with age during maintenance, partially offsetting performance decline. Therefore, interventions to boost VSTM in older adults might target compensatory frontoparietal representations during memory maintenance, and readout of untapped visual representations at recall.

piezas.resumenOriginal: Objective Vestibular migraine (VM) has been associated with central sensory processing abnormalities and neural hyperexcitability, which may disrupt temporal coding despite normal peripheral hearing. This study aimed to determine whether auditory temporal processing is differentially affected in VM by comparing temporal resolution and temporal masking abilities with those of healthy controls. Methods This cross-sectional study included 17 adults aged 20-50 years with definite VM and 17 age- and sex-matched healthy controls. All participants had normal hearing sensitivity and normal cognitive function, confirmed using the Standardized Mini-Mental State Examination (SMMSE). Auditory temporal processing was evaluated using the Gap Detection Test (GDT) and the Forward Masking Test (FMT). Group differences were analyzed using appropriate statistical methods. Results No significant differences were observed between the groups regarding age or sex. Participants with VM demonstrated significantly poorer GDT performance compared with healthy controls, indicating impaired auditory temporal resolution (p 0.05). Conclusions Individuals with VM exhibit selective impairment of auditory temporal processing despite normal peripheral hearing. These findings support the inclusion of central auditory temporal processing assessment as part of the comprehensive audiological evaluation of this population and suggest that auditory training targeting temporal processing deficits may represent a potential avenue for future rehabilitation. piezas.titulo: Peer Mentoring Benefits in Rehabilitation for Individuals With Spinal Cord Injury: A Systematic Review.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Importance The lived experiences of peer mentors with spinal cord injury (SCI) provide distinct value in the rehabilitation process and contribute to improved outcomes. When combined with traditional therapy, peer mentorship programs can enhance life satisfaction among individuals living with SCI. Objective To explore the impact that peer-led mentorship programs and interventions have on the rehabilitation outcomes for individuals with a spinal cord injury (SCI). Data sources PubMed, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, CINAHL, ERIC, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, MedNar, and OpenGrey were searched between 2014 and 2024. The Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool was adapted and used to assess risk of bias in the included studies. Study selection and data collection Inclusion criteria included individuals with SCI who participated in peer mentorship and reported outcomes on quality of life, well-being, independence, or activities of daily living (ADLs) or instrumental ADLs. Exclusion criteria included interventions conducted via telehealth or reported outcomes of social participation. Findings Five articles were analyzed for synthesis, which included individuals 18 yr and older with an SCI. Findings support peer mentorship as an important component of rehabilitation. Findings may have limited generalizability across different settings and populations because of the small number of available studies and variability in study designs, interventions, and outcome measures. None of the articles reviewed included occupational therapists. Conclusions and relevance This review highlighted the benefits of peer mentorship in enhanced life satisfaction. Findings support peer mentorship as an important component of rehabilitation. Future research should examine the benefits of incorporating peer-led intervention programs across the continuum of care, including occupational therapy, in enhancing best practices in SCI rehabilitation. Plain-Language Summary: Peer mentorship programs can help people with spinal cord injuries adjust to daily life by providing guidance, support, and encouragement that professionals without lived experience may not offer. This review found that peer mentoring can improve psychological well-being and health management and reduce unplanned hospital visits. Evidence is limited because of the small number of studies and variations in study design; however, the results suggest that meaningful benefits may be present. Further research is needed to determine the most effective way to implement peer mentorship across rehabilitation settings.

piezas.titulo: Two Nonprofits Join Forces to Support Adolescents on Autism Spectrum
piezas.resumenOriginal: Two Nonprofits Join Forces to Support Adolescents on Autism Spectrum STAR Admin Thu, 06/15/2017 - 14:07 STAR Institute for Sensory Processing Disorder (SPD) and T.A.C.T. (Teaching the Autism Community Trades) are two Colorado nonprofits who have partnered to create a series of respite camps serving adolescents who have autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Developmental Pathways has awarded the organizations a $25,000 grant to fund three F.U.S.E. (Fostering Unlimited Success and Empowerment) camps through 2018. STAR Institute offers premier treatment for SPD and brings expertise in social skills while T.AC.T. teaches trade and life skills to individuals with ASD and SPD with an emphasis on fostering independence and personal growth. “This is a very rare and exciting way to see two nonprofits interact. Our partnership to create F.U.S.E. allows both of our organizations to combine expertise in a way that best serves these adolescents to find new interests and gain the soft skills to successfully participate in peer groups and future workplaces”, says Dick Layton, Director of STAR Institute for SPD. The respite camps will be week-long day camps that host six students per camp ages 12-15 who have autism spectrum disorder. The camps will teach pre-vocational and vocational skills in a supportive, social, and inclusionary environment. Each camp has a different project for participants including: building a non-motorized go-cart with a partner, building an instrument to play in a band, and crafting board games. “The intended focus of F.U.S.E. is not just about offering a respite program for families. By generating new experiences for these adolescents, we hope to foster new skills, new interests, develop social skills, and give them a sense of empowerment to participate in what hopefully becomes a new hobby or future career interest”, says Danny Combs co-founder and president of T.A.C.T. SPD is a neurological disorder that disrupts the way an individual processes and responds to sensations. The disorder can affect people in only one sense–for example, just touch or just sight or just movement–or in multiple senses. One person with SPD may over-respond to touch sensation and find clothing, physical contact, other tactile sensory input to be unbearable and/or they may respond to visual or auditory or another sensory input. Another person might under-respond and show little or no reaction to stimulation, even pain or extreme hot and cold or just may be slow to respond to sensation. SPD and ASD have a high co-morbidity rate, but are also found to be standalone disorders. ASD refers to conditions categorized by challenges with social skills, repetitive behaviors, speech and nonverbal communication, as well as by unique strengths and differences that can occur on a range from mild to severe. Individuals with ASD and SPD frequently struggle with interpersonal skills over their lifetime and are often underestimated, which can lead to specific difficulty in career and relationships. F.U.S.E. aims to give individuals the ability to ignite new interests and feel empowered in group collaboration, which can lead to greater success in career and relationships. About STAR Institute for Sensory Processing Disorder: The STAR Institute for Sensory Processing Disorder, a Colorado 501(c)(3), is the world leader in treatment, research, and education for Sensory Processing Disorder, a neurological condition that disrupts the daily lives of more than 4 million Americans. The STAR Institute is the premier treatment center for children, adults and families living with Sensory Processing Disorder, feeding disorders, and other sensory conditions associated with ADHD, autism, and other developmental disorders. Dr. Lucy Jane Miller, founder of STAR Institute, is widely recognized as the leader in Sensory Processing Disorder research worldwide. For more information about the Greenwood Village, Colorado clinic, visit http://www.spdSTAR.org or call 303-221-7827. About T.A.C.T. piezas.titulo: Traditional and religious treatments administered to children with autism spectrum disorder in South Africa: a qualitative study of practices, composition and risk
piezas.resumenOriginal: IntroductionThe appraisal of treatments for autism spectrum disorder (ASD) has largely focused on interventions delivered within formal healthcare systems, particularly in high-income settings. In South Africa, children with ASD may receive concurrent care from hospitals, traditional health practitioners and religious leaders, yet the practices administered outside formal healthcare remain poorly documented. This study aimed to identify these practices and interpret their potential risks in relation to published evidence of harm.MethodsA qualitative study was conducted at a public tertiary hospital in Soweto, Johannesburg. Semi-structured interviews were undertaken with 24 parents and caregivers and 10 hospital clinicians, alongside two focus groups involving traditional health practitioners and religious leaders, respectively. As practitioner participants did not recognise the term autism, they were briefed on its DSM-5 features before discussing practices previously administered to children presenting with similar characteristics. Their accounts therefore did not necessarily concern children with confirmed ASD diagnoses. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis, followed by deductive recoding of reported practices into a route-of-administration taxonomy.ResultsTwenty-five distinct practices were identified. All children in the sample had received at least one intervention outside formal healthcare, with most receiving several alongside hospital treatment. Ingested and rectally administered preparations presented particular safety concerns because their constituents were undisclosed, dosing relied on clinical impression and paediatric formulations were unavailable. Neither caregivers nor clinicians could identify the substances administered, while practitioners declined to disclose their composition. Practitioners categorised ASD-related presentations within a broader conception of insanity, and one non-clinician proposed cutting tissue beneath a child's tongue to facilitate speech. Reported benefits, including explanatory frameworks, family connectedness and sustained hope, related primarily to caregivers' experiences rather than documented therapeutic improvements in children.DiscussionThe findings identify potentially harmful and insufficiently documented interventions administered alongside formal ASD care. Their safety cannot be adequately assessed without information about their constituents and administration. Route-based risk triage, non-punitive disclosure during clinical consultations and protected constituent disclosure are recommended. As the study was conducted at a single urban tertiary hospital, its findings are context-specific and should not be generalised beyond the setting investigated.

piezas.titulo: Fragments: September 16
piezas.resumenOriginal: Reports of agentic hacking continue, in this case it happened back in May and it seems OpenAI did not disclose that they were responsible. Simon Willison sees two options: After the Hugging Face and Wiki attacks OpenAI were still unable to review their previous logs and determine that they had previously attacked RubyGems. They knew about the attack on RubyGems and made the decision not to reach out to the RubyGems team about it. Both of these are bad! Given this incident, the Hugging Face situation, and the Wiki attack, the obvious question right now is how many more incidents like this are out there waiting to be discovered? ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Dave Farley: Stop asking the sci-fi question: ‘Is it conscious?’ Start asking the engineering question: ‘Is this a powerful, unpredictable component being put somewhere consequential, and where’s the feedback that tells us that it’s safe? ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Nate Silver is known for his forecasts, but to do them he writes a lot of code for his models. He’s found agentic engineering capable of doing miraculous work . In spending so much time with the LLMs, I’m super attentive to improvements in their capabilities. And these changes tend not to be so linear. Instead, they improve in step functions, almost as phase changes. Suddenly, the models just start doing things capably that they were screwing up before. In my experience, there was a big leap forward when reasoning models first came out in late 2024/early 2025 — enough that they were occasionally useful for tasks involving data and not just words — and then another one this past winter. The most recent changes I’ve noticed, however, have had less to do with intelligence and more with persistence. Consider the Hugging Face attack. Although these agents showed remarkable intelligence, they weren’t really super-intelligent - but they were super-persistent. This is a common theme of AI in its various forms: Game engines like AlphaGo Zero start out by basically making random moves — but by playing against themselves millions of times, they eventually far surpass human capabilities As we try to figure out what kind of regulations we need to keep AI under control, we need to remember that we should design our guards around super-persistence as much as worrying about super-intelligence. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ “Uncle Bob” Martin has made many posts on X during the last few months about his programming with LLMs. His approach has been to build a firm harness to keep them under control, so they create software that is maintainable as well as functional. Sadly the posts have been frustratingly light on detail. But now it seems that lack of information may not matter And while I was heads-down getting that to work, the agents got a LOT better. So much so that when I came up for air, the need for my harness was obviated. Indeed, the need for any but the most liberal of harnesses may be obviated. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Some tidbits that struck me from Ezra Klein’s recent (recommended) interview with Matt Sheehan on the interplay between regulation of AI and competition with China . While Chinese models have made some surprisingly remarkable gains in the slipstream of US frontier models, the US still has 8 times as much compute available to it than China - which is a material gap. People in the US worry that regulation will slow down the US model builders, but these rapid recent gains in China have occurred under much more regulation Americans say that when they set up a hotline to talk to Chinese leaders in a crisis, the Chinese don’t pick up the phone. But this misunderstands the Chinese system. Individual Chinese, even powerful ones, aren’t given individual decision-making power. They operate with committees and documents. So the Americans are better off sending a fax than trying to call an individual Like so many things, effective regulation needs regular practice When American policymakers are like: Where do you start? — I sometimes say: Well, you start by starting. You learn how to regulate things, you learn how to legislate on them by regulating and legislating on them.

piezas.resumenOriginal: Today’s engineers face an unprecedented acceleration in AI hardware complexity, as explained in the recent research article “ Revisiting Edge AI: Opportunities and Challenges .” The article examines the rapid growth of edge AI and the challenges it creates, including resource constraints, model architecture limitations, and network demands across edge-AI deployments. The acceleration is driven by a fundamental shift in how modern AI models are built and scaled. As the models have become much larger and more complex, they are computationally more demanding because they contain more parameters and require more calculations. To meet the demands of scaling deep neural networks, the industry is increasingly developing AI chips that are designed for specific tasks. One major reason is that moving data between memory and the processor has become a major limitation on AI performance. The movement to confront the hardware bottleneck—the AI memory wall —has altered the trajectory of semiconductor innovation, shifting architectural priorities toward domain-specific accelerator platforms. No longer can engineers evaluate systems statically; they must master joint hardware design and network-algorithm co-optimization to navigate the critical trade‑offs between throughput, latency, and operational efficiency. The challenges are addressed in the new AI Processor Architecture, Design Principles, and Performance program , developed by IEEE Educational Activities with support from the IEEE Computer Society . Topics covered The five-course program provides a structured exploration of AI processor technologies, from fundamental design principles to advanced architectures and real-world deployment. The topics are: Fundamental principles of design and functionality. Practical insights into advanced architectures. Understanding neural processing units for industry deployment. Emerging trends and evolving architectures. Designing for edge, cloud, quantum, and the Internet of Things (IoT). The program addresses the needs of professionals across the AI hardware ecosystem, including hardware architects, chip designers, embedded systems developers, data‑center hardware engineers, and innovators exploring next‑generation processor ecosystems. It is also valuable for those transitioning into AI chip design or seeking to understand the architectural forces shaping modern machine learning acceleration. For many, it provides the bridge between theoretical knowledge and the collaborative, cross‑disciplinary reasoning required in engineering environments. The program is designed to explore how modern AI processors are conceived, structured, and optimized. The architectural layers that define contemporary AI hardware will be covered, including compute units, memory hierarchies, dataflows, and the performance characteristics that emerge from design decisions. The curriculum bridges theory and application, enabling participants to interpret architectural foundations, analyze trade‑offs, and understand how hardware structures shape computational efficiency across diverse environments. By the end of the courses, learners will be able to evaluate processor behavior with the analytical precision expected of professionals working at the frontier of AI hardware design. The simulated storytelling and dialogues make advanced engineering concepts approachable without sacrificing depth or interactivity, because the user is occasionally challenged to decide the correct answer that leads to the best course of action. A hardware engineer might push back against a systems engineer’s demands, for example, revealing the friction between physical constraints and algorithmic ambition. A computational validation specialist might interrogate a chip performance engineer’s optimism, exposing the gap between theoretical throughput and real‑world behavior. A heterogeneous systems architect could debate a multiprocessor coordination specialist about synchronization overheads, while a standards development engineer discusses regulatory implications with a technology strategy and compliance architect. By the end of the course, learners will be able to evaluate processor behavior with the analytical precision expected of professionals working at the frontier of AI hardware design. piezas.titulo: Building a multiplayer game world with autonomous Fable-class models
piezas.resumenOriginal: How I Built the Most AI-Pilled Company in the World Don't be put off by the clickbait headline, this piece by Jacob Sansbury describing how they are building Spawn is a fascinating exploration of the bleeding edge of what's possible with agentic engineering against frontier models. Spawn is a massively multiplayer gaming environment where players can use prompts (to the in-game agent, Savi) to modify the game world. I fired it up on my phone for a few minutes and was able to prompt a castle into existence, then a dragon, then ride the dragon to fly around that castle. By Jacob's telling, Spawn is now being developed autonomously by a swarm of Fable-powered agents costing over $3 million in tokens per month ("we spend 30x payroll on AI tokens"). Our agents change the live code directly and ship to production hourly, so they read every error, bug report and metric themselves. About 60% of our work starts from a production error, a Savi bug report (Savi is the AI you build games with in Spawn), something odd in our logs, or a feature request. Savi files bugs herself. When a user hits one, or Savi hits one in the product, she files it. It goes straight to an agent that decides whether it's a real bug to fix, something we won't fix, or intentional design that needs a decision. Usually it becomes a change, delivered to that user within an hour, with a message in the same chat. This is continuous deployment turned up to 11: A loop this tight only works if it never stops, so we treat an hour without a ship as a SEV-0, our most severe kind of incident. Unshipped changes pile up, and every problem already in production lasts longer. The feedback slows down too. An agent can only keep a few hours of work in its head, so shipping faster than that actually helps it stay coherent. [...] We can roll back a broken change in 30 seconds, exactly where it's broken and nowhere else. When a monitor or a log alert fires, it starts or wakes an agent that owns the incident, and we break things on purpose to test that those recovery paths work. My eyebrows raised at least a dozen times reading this. I have trouble imagining this style of development working on software with higher stakes for when something goes wrong, but for a game this appears to be working surprisingly well. Jacob says that Fable 5 (and then 5.1) was the model that made this level of autonomy possible. Opus 5.5 doesn't quite hack it for them, and when they tried GPT-6 Astra to apply fixes from a security review everything stopped working: Every feature had been disabled and marked to be turned on again once the security fixes were done. Astra had gone through our whole product and made the insecure things secure by turning them off. These kinds of extreme experiments are why I'm excited about game development as a substrate for exploring the edges of what today's coding agents can do. piezas.titulo: Designing Memory Architecture for Stateful AI Agents: Short-Term Context and Long-Term Persistence
piezas.resumenOriginal: A language model holds nothing between calls. Each request arrives with no memory of the previous one, and the model responds from the prompt in front of it and nothing more. For a one-shot question, that is fine. For an agent a person returns to across days, threads, and separate tasks, it becomes the defining design constraint. The behavior users expect from an agent, recalling what they said last week, resuming a task that stalled, applying their stated preferences without being asked again, is precisely the behavior a stateless model cannot produce on its own. A large language model (LLM) does not forget your context because it chose to. It never had it. The reflex fix is to paste the history back in. Keep a buffer of prior turns and prepend it to every prompt, so the agent looks like it remembers. That illusion survives a short demo and breaks in production. Building stateful AI agents that hold continuity across sessions takes a memory architecture, not a bigger buffer.

piezas.titulo: Imaging findings and clinical outcomes in neonates with isolated subependymal echogenicity on cranial ultrasound: a retrospective cohort study
piezas.resumenOriginal: ObjectiveTo describe clinical and imaging findings in neonates with isolated subependymal echogenicity on cranial ultrasound and examine associations with recorded mortality and cerebral palsy.MethodsThis retrospective single-center cohort included 317 neonates admitted between January 2015 and December 2018 with an initial ultrasound finding suspicious for isolated subependymal hemorrhage. Clinical records, available MRI findings, and follow-up information were reviewed. Cerebral palsy was ascertained from rehabilitation or neurology diagnostic records, supplemented by telephone follow-up in January 2026, independently of developmental test scores. The primary adjusted analysis compared death with all survivors using an exploratory six-item comorbidity count and clinical covariates; hospitalization duration was excluded, and laterality was coded as unilateral or bilateral.ResultsThere were 52 deaths (16.4%), 9 survivors with recorded cerebral palsy (2.8%), and 256 survivors without recorded cerebral palsy (80.8%). MRI findings were compatible with hemorrhage in 61 of 90 examined infants (67.8%). In the complete-case mortality model (n = 316), each additional comorbidity was associated with greater odds of death (adjusted OR, 2.462; 95% CI, 1.787–3.391; p < 0.001). The other included covariates were not statistically significant. White matter abnormalities were recorded in nine infants, including eight of the nine infants with cerebral palsy and one without recorded cerebral palsy.ConclusionSystemic comorbidity burden was associated with mortality within this ultrasound-defined cohort. White matter abnormalities accompanied most recorded cerebral palsy cases, but this observation remains descriptive. Specialist diagnostic records and later telephone follow-up characterize persistent clinical diagnoses; they do not establish the independent effect of subependymal echogenicity or normal development across all domains in survivors without cerebral palsy.

piezas.titulo: Disrupting SORL1-retromer endosomal recycling in mice drives the age-dependent neurodegenerative signature of Alzheimer's disease
piezas.resumenOriginal: MRI studies have mapped the atrophic signature that distinguishes Alzheimer's disease (AD), isolating regions differentially vulnerable to its age-dependent neurodegenerative process. We test the hypothesis that an endosomal recycling pathway regulated by the interaction of SORL1 with retromer, which is pathogenically disrupted in AD, might drive the neurodegenerative process via multiple yearlong studies in over 140 wildtype and SORL1 deficient mice, modeling AD's causative mutations. MRI studies revealed that SORL1 deficiency induced an age-dependent AD-pattern of atrophy, centered on the trans-entorhinal cortex, and that atrophy was prevented by SORL1 restoration, secondary to overexpressing the retromer protein VPS26b. Postmortem studies validated that the atrophy reflects neuronal loss. Proteomic profiling revealed that the atrophy is associated with reductions in cell death suppressors, one of which was then found deficient in the trans-entorhinal cortex of AD patients. Besides supporting the hypothesis, taken together with other findings, the results suggest that SORL1-retromer disruptions represent a therapeutically-amenable common 'neurodegeneration pathway' in AD.

piezas.titulo: Disrupted Top-Down Modulation as a Mechanism of Impaired Multisensory Processing in Autistic Children.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Atypical sensory processing is commonly observed in autism, particularly when integration across sensory modalities is required. The neural mechanisms underlying multisensory differences remain unclear. We recorded EEG while autistic children aged 8-13 (AU;n = 40), siblings of autistic children (SIB;n = 26), and non-autistic controls (NA;n = 36) performed a simple reaction-time task to auditory (A), visual (V), and audiovisual (AV) stimuli. Analyses targeted event-related potentials (ERPs), alpha-band event-related desynchronization (α-ERD), and long-range theta-band functional connectivity. Groups did not differ across unisensory measures, indicating comparable unisensory processing. By contrast, multisensory integration (MSI;AV-(A+V)) differed across groups: NA children showed significant ERP MSI over parieto-central sites that was absent in AU and SIB; and α-ERD MSI was significantly reduced in AU, with SIB showing an intermediate profile. Connectivity analyses revealed reduced AV fronto-parieto-occipital coupling in autistic children relative to non-autistic children, suggesting weaker large-scale coordination during multisensory processing. These results point to a multisensory-specific deficit spanning early sensory encoding, posterior α-ERD, and fronto-posterior coupling and support disrupted multisensory influences on sensory processing due to reduced multisensory attentional orienting. SIB profiles suggest inherited liability for these neural phenotypes. These results help explain well-documented behavioral MSI differences in autism by linking impaired early enhancement with attenuated top-down control of sensory cortex.

piezas.titulo: How Top-Down Are We? Reconsidering the Gap Between Occupational Therapy's Identity and Practice.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Occupational therapy has spent more than a century defining occupation as its professional core. Yet studies across countries and settings show a recurring gap. Therapists value occupation-centered practice while often relying on impairment-focused assessment and intervention. This article argues that the profession may face a translation problem more than an identity problem. Biomedical service structures, standardized measurement, workplace culture, and professional socialization can pull reasoning toward body functions. Bottom-up methods are not inherently incompatible with occupational therapy; the problem arises when change in a component is treated as sufficient evidence of occupational success. Drawing on occupational therapy research, the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health, rehabilitation science, and disability rights, we argue that occupation and participation should remain the outcomes that organize assessment, intervention, and evaluation. Practical changes are proposed for clinical reasoning, outcome measurement, education, supervision, and service design.

piezas.titulo: Occupational therapy interventions for functional neurological disorder: a scoping review
piezas.resumenOriginal: IntroductionFunctional Neurological Disorder (FND) is a common and disabling condition for which multidisciplinary rehabilitation is recommended; however, the specific contribution of occupational therapy remains poorly defined. This scoping review aimed to map and characterize occupational therapy interventions for people with FND, examine how these are delivered and evaluated within rehabilitation and identify priorities for future research.MethodsA scoping review was conducted using Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology. Peer-reviewed English-language intervention studies involving adults (≥18 years) with FND who received occupational therapy delivered independently or as part of multidisciplinary rehabilitation and reporting treatment outcomes were included. Descriptive analysis was undertaken. OVID Medline, Embase, APA PsycInfo and CINAHL Plus were searched from inception to July 2026, supplemented by reference list screening.ResultsForty-one studies (n= 1,284 participants; sample sizes 1–201) were included, with only one randomized study. Occupational therapy was predominantly delivered within multidisciplinary rehabilitation; only one study included a subgroup receiving occupational therapy alone. Despite considerable variation in intervention reporting, common occupational therapy intervention components included facilitating occupational engagement, movement retraining and anxiety management, with symptom management strategies integrated into functional activities to promote confidence and independence. Improvements in symptom severity, functional ability, mental health, and quality of life were reported following multidisciplinary rehabilitation including occupational therapy. However, findings were primarily derived from uncontrolled studies, and interpretation was further limited by heterogeneity in intervention approaches, inconsistent use of outcome measures, and variable follow-up.DiscussionAlthough occupational therapy was included in all eligible studies, occupational therapy-specific interventions and associated outcomes were inconsistently described and evaluated, limiting understanding of occupational therapy's distinct contribution within multidisciplinary rehabilitation. Future research should focus on clearly defining and evaluating the components of occupational therapy interventions.

piezas.titulo: Somatostatin-excitatory coordination emerges with dexterous motor skill learning
piezas.resumenOriginal: Motor skill-learning increases spatio-temporal consistency in neuronal activity in primary motor cortex (M1), and Somatostatin-expressing (SST) interneurons are causally involved in these learning-related activity changes. Yet, how SST-excitatory interactions shape population level activity changes during motor skill acquisition is still unknown. Here, we imaged large populations of excitatory neurons and identified SST or parvalbumin-expressing (PV) interneurons across successive days as mice learned a dexterous, persistently M1-dependent reach-to-grasp task. Sparse, temporally coordinated, trial-resolved, and rate-controlled functional interactions between SST neurons and skill-modulated excitatory neurons emerged with learning and were stronger than those in excitatory-excitatory or PV-excitatory pairs. Interactions strengthened as neurons were recruited to the skill-modulated ensemble and weakened when skill modulation was lost. SST activity also became temporally reliable earlier than excitatory or PV activity, and SST consistency was significantly associated with behavioral performance even after controlling for training session number. Additionally, SST neurons carried more information about movement kinematics than randomly selected subsets of excitatory neurons. Overall, SST neurons became selectively coordinated with behaviorally relevant excitatory populations, revealing a cell-type-specific functional architecture for dexterous motor learning.

piezas.titulo: Prefrontal cortical morphometric covariance and cognitive task performance in healthy young adults: an exploratory analysis of Human Connectome Project data
piezas.resumenOriginal: The prefrontal cortex (PFC) is implicated in many cognitive tasks, including working memory, reward-based decision-making, executive control, and metacognition. This exploratory analysis investigated whether individual expression of PFC cortical thickness and surface area covariance components is associated with cognitive task performance. The sample comprised Human Connectome Project (HCP) MRI data from 743 healthy adults (age 22–36+). Oblimin-rotated principal component analysis (PCA) was applied to residualized thickness and surface area for 22 PFC regions, controlling for age, sex, and ICV. Component scores were entered as predictors in separate regression models for the Flanker Age-Adjusted Score (inhibitory control), the Gambling RT Difference (RT for the same “larger” guess in reward minus punishment blocks), and 2-Back median RT (working memory speed). Parallel analysis favored two thickness components; a prespecified three-component solution (Global/Lateral PFC, RC1; Orbitofrontal, RC2; Anterior Cingulate, RC3; 53.7% of variance) was retained by decision, and RC1 and RC2 were only moderately stable across bootstrap resamples. RC1 was nominally associated with lower Flanker scores (β = −0.103, p = 0.027), opposite to the predicted direction, and RC2 with a smaller Gambling RT Difference (β = −0.103, p = 0.025); neither survived false discovery rate (FDR) correction (q = 0.054). In uncorrected models added at review, whole-cortex mean thickness alone robustly predicted Flanker scores but not the Gambling RT Difference; neither component association survived regressing mean thickness out before PCA. In surface area analyses, greater orbitofrontal surface area (AC2) was associated with faster 2-Back RT (β = −0.125, p = 0.003; q = 0.032 across 12 surface area tests and 0.064 across all 24 component tests), not explained by a speed-accuracy tradeoff. This unpredicted association persisted in most sensitivity analyses but was attenuated and non-significant when total surface area was regressed out before PCA (β = −0.065, p = 0.078). In conclusion, no prefrontal-specific association was robust. Global cortical thickness accounts for the Flanker association more parsimoniously, the Gambling RT Difference association was not robust under either account, and the orbitofrontal surface area association could not be separated from global surface area; all associations require replication.

destilado.texto: Encontrar que mayor superficie orbitofrontal acelera la respuesta en la prueba de 2‑Back altera la idea de la corteza prefrontal. El estudio del Human Connectome Project, publicado en Frontiers, muestra una asociación nominal que no supera la corrección, pero abre la puerta a entrenamientos cognitivos.

piezas.titulo: Opening the Black Box of Ayres Sensory Integration<sup>®</sup>: Clarifying Mechanisms of Change from Treatment Theory to Participation.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Ayres Sensory Integration ® (ASI) remains one of the most widely used and debated intervention approaches in occupational therapy and related disciplines. Recent advances in rehabilitation treatment specification and reporting frameworks, including the Rehabilitation Treatment Specification System (RTSS) and the Reporting Guideline for Intervention Description in Rehabilitation (GUIDE-Rehab), emphasize the need for precise articulation of treatment ingredients, mechanisms of action, and targets. However, interventions grounded in neurodevelopmental theories, such as Ayres' theory of sensory integration, are complex, and may present challenges when interpreted within linear causal models. This paper argues that ASI theory is best understood as a treatment theory targeting proximal sensory-motor capacities, while participation-level outcomes may be more comprehensively explained through an enablement framework. Integrating this perspective with data-driven decision making (DDDM) clarifies longstanding ambiguities in the ASI literature and strengthens intervention specification, evaluation, and interpretation.

piezas.titulo: Lifestyle Documentation in Therapy Evaluations for Autistic Children: A Lexicon-Based Analysis of Electronic Health Records.
piezas.resumenOriginal: BackgroundWhole person health (WPH) is a multidimensional construct encompassing, physical, and mental health along with relational constructs such as social health that are deeply tied to well-being. Autistic individuals report an overall lower quality of life, but the extent to which these issues are addressed during therapy evaluations has not been examined systematically.MethodologyIn this retrospective, cross-sectional study, we employ a rule-based NLP/lexicon-based approach to examine the areas of focus of therapy evaluations documented by occupational therapy, physical therapy (PT), and speech-language pathology (SLP) professionals. Using electronic health records for children aged 2 to 18 diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) (n = 5619 evaluation reports of n = 2021 unique patients), we classified health records based on the domains addressed.ResultsAcross notes, nutrition had the highest average degree of documentation ( M = 2.14), compared to activity ( M = 0.91), followed by wellness ( M = 0.66), and sleep ( M = 0.39). In occupational therapy, wellness was the most common (77.62% of notes), followed by physical activity (76.49% of notes), nutrition management (73.33% of notes), and sleep (34.97% of notes). The overall area under the curve (AUC) from the receiver operating characteristic analysis is 0.89.ConclusionsWhile it is encouraging that most evaluations addressed nutrition or physical activity, the near absence of attention to sleep represents a critical gap in care. Given sleep's foundational role in overall health and daily functioning, its omission is particularly concerning. Occupational therapists and interdisciplinary rehabilitation teams should more deliberately integrate WPH frameworks into their evaluations.
